concept.name: Contract for difference
concept.definition: A leveraged over-the-counter derivative between a client and a provider in which the parties exchange the difference between the opening and closing price of an underlying asset — a share, index, currency, or commodity — without either party owning the underlying. The FCA classifies CFDs as complex, high-risk products that carry a considerable risk of substantial losses.
concept.intuition: A CFD is a cash-settled bet on a price move: you gain or lose the full change in the asset's price while posting only a fraction of its value as margin.
concept.mechanics: A position is opened with initial margin; profit or loss equals the price change times position size, and long positions pay daily financing on the full notional. Regulators such as the FCA restrict retail leverage (between 30:1 and 2:1 depending on the underlying), mandate margin close-out, and provide negative balance protection for retail clients.
concept.formula: PnL (long) = (P_close - P_open) x quantity, minus financing and any commissions.
concept.failure_modes: High leverage means small adverse moves can wipe out the deposit quickly; a large majority of retail CFD accounts lose money. The client also bears provider counterparty risk, and overnight financing charges erode positions held for long periods.
concept.misconceptions: That a CFD confers ownership or voting rights in the underlying — it is purely a price-difference contract. Also, stop-losses do not guarantee an exit price in gapping markets.
concept.example: Buying 1,000 share CFDs at GBP 10.00 with 20% margin requires GBP 2,000; if the price rises to GBP 10.50, the gain is GBP 500 minus financing — a 25% return on margin from a 5% price move, with symmetric downside.

citations.source: UK Financial Conduct Authority, press release: FCA warns investors in CFDs risk losing out on protections
citations.section: Notes to editors: definition and risk characterization of CFDs
